context_blurb:
Every stone you pick up has a long past. The pebble in your hand may once have been melted rock, then sand on the sea floor, then rock squeezed deep underground. Earth keeps turning one kind of rock into another, so slowly that a single change can take millions of years. That endless remaking is called the rock cycle.

Geologists, the scientists who study rocks, sort every rock into one of three great kinds, and what decides its kind is how the rock formed, not how it looks. Igneous rock, named from the Latin word for fire, forms when melted rock cools and hardens. Sedimentary rock forms from sediment, loose bits of rock, sand and shell, pressed and cemented together. Metamorphic rock forms when an older rock is changed by heat and pressure. Colour can fool you: a dark rock might be igneous basalt, sedimentary coal or metamorphic slate.

Melted rock underground is called magma; once it pours out at the surface it is lava. Look closely at granite and you can pick out its crystals with your bare eyes, pale grains and dark specks, while the crystals in dark basalt are far too small to see. The difference comes from how fast the melted rock cooled, because crystals need time to grow.

Granite's magma cooled slowly, kilometres underground, over hundreds of thousands of years, so its crystals grew large. Basalt's lava cooled quickly at the surface, so its crystals stayed tiny. Basalt is the commonest igneous rock at Earth's surface, and most of the solid rock under the open ocean is basalt, from lava that welled out onto the sea floor and hardened there. Granite, by contrast, is common in the crust of the continents. Some lava cools so fast that it hardens into obsidian, a glossy black natural glass with almost no crystals at all.

Granite hardens kilometres down, so how do whole cliffs of it come to stand in the open air? Over millions of years the land is slowly pushed up while rain, rivers and ice wear away the rock on top of the granite, until rock that hardened far below lies bare. Granite does not come out of volcanoes: it is magma that stayed below and hardened there.

Heat and pressure deep underground can remake a rock without melting it. A rock turns metamorphic while it stays solid: the heat and pressure make its crystals regrow, often larger than before, and the rock comes out denser and more compact. Many people think metamorphic rock melts along the way, but it does not; rock that melted would become magma, and then igneous rock.

Where hot magma forces its way into limestone, a rock built from the shells and coral of warm, shallow seas, the heat bakes the nearby limestone into marble. Its small crystals grow larger as it bakes, and marble has been a favourite stone for statues and buildings for thousands of years.

Slate begins as shale, a sedimentary rock made of hardened mud. Mild heat and pressure turn and regrow its flat flakes of clay until they all lie the same way, which is why slate peels apart into smooth, thin sheets, good for roofs and for the writing slates of old schoolrooms.

In granite, pale and dark crystals are sprinkled through the rock with no pattern at all. Buried deep for ages, granite can become gneiss (said like "nice"), a metamorphic rock with stripes. Deep heat and pressure sort granite's light and dark minerals into separate layers, and those layers show as bands.

Rock travels around the cycle by many paths, in no fixed order: any of the three kinds can become either of the other two, through melting, weathering, or heat and pressure. Far beneath a mountain range, metamorphic rock can heat up until it starts to melt, and the molten part creeps upward and sets as granite. Whatever a rock was before, anything that hardens from melted rock is igneous, so here metamorphic rock has become igneous rock.

For basalt, or any rock, to become sedimentary rock, it must first be worn down by weathering: rain, ice, waves and wind break it into bits called sediment, which can then be buried, pressed and cemented into new rock.
